context.concept_name: Measures of central tendency (mean, median, mode)

coverage.learning_objective: Compute the mean, median, and mode of a dataset and choose which one best represents its typical (central) value, especially when the data is skewed.

required_facts.statement: The sample mean is computed as the sum of the observed values divided by the number of observations.
The median is the middle value when the data are ordered from smallest to largest; if there is an even number of observations, the median is the average of the two middle values.
The mode is the value that occurs most often in the data; there can be more than one mode.

The mean is more strongly affected by extreme observations (such as those in the tail of a skewed distribution) than the median, which is more robust to them; for this reason the median can better represent a typical value in a skewed dataset.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine a batch of seven delivery orders whose delivery times, in minutes, are 18, 20, 22, 22, 26, 28, and 80. Before you can say anything useful about this batch, you need one number that answers "what's typical here?" -- and there are three different ways to compute that number.

The sample mean is computed as the sum of the observed values divided by the number of observations. For the seven delivery times, the sum is 18+20+22+22+26+28+80 = 216, and 216 divided by 7 is about 30.9 minutes.

The median is the middle value when the data are ordered from smallest to largest; if there is an even number of observations, the median is the average of the two middle values. Sorted, the seven times are 18, 20, 22, 22, 26, 28, 80 -- the middle (fourth) value is 22 minutes.
The mode is the value that occurs most often in the data; there can be more than one mode. In this batch, 22 minutes appears twice while every other value appears once, so 22 is the mode.

Notice that the mean (about 30.9 minutes) sits well above the median and mode (both 22 minutes). That gap exists because the mean is more strongly affected by extreme observations (such as those in the tail of a skewed distribution) than the median, which is more robust to them; for this reason the median can better represent a typical value in a skewed dataset. Here, the single 80-minute delivery pulls the mean upward far more than it moves the median, so 22 minutes -- not 30.9 -- is the more representative "typical" delivery time for this batch.

Mean, median, and mode all try to answer "what's typical," but they compute it differently, and the mean and median react differently to a batch that includes one unusually large value -- so before reporting a single center number, it's worth checking whether an extreme value like that 80-minute delivery is pulling the mean away from where most of the data actually sits.

context.concept_name: Measures of spread (range, variance, standard deviation)

coverage.learning_objective: Compute the range, variance, and standard deviation of a dataset and interpret what each says about how spread out the data are.

required_facts.statement: The range of a data set is the largest value minus the smallest value.

The variance is computed by taking each observation's deviation from the mean, squaring it, summing the squared deviations, and dividing by n - 1 (one less than the number of observations); it is roughly the average squared distance of the observations from the mean.
The standard deviation is the square root of the variance, and it describes the typical distance of an observation from the mean.

The standard deviation is expressed in the same units as the original data, while the variance is expressed in squared units; the range is based only on the two most extreme values and ignores how the rest of the data are spread.

teaching_blocks.content: Knowing the typical delivery time (22 minutes, from the median) doesn't say how spread out the batch is. Most of the seven delivery times (18, 20, 22, 22, 26, 28, 80 minutes) cluster fairly close together, but one sits far away -- spread measures capture that difference.
The range of a data set is the largest value minus the smallest value. For this batch, that's 80 minus 18, or 62 minutes.

The variance is computed by taking each observation's deviation from the mean, squaring it, summing the squared deviations, and dividing by n - 1 (one less than the number of observations); it is roughly the average squared distance of the observations from the mean. With a mean of about 30.9 minutes, the seven squared deviations sum to about 2886.9, and dividing by n - 1 = 6 gives a variance of about 481.1 (in minutes squared).

The standard deviation is the square root of the variance, and it describes the typical distance of an observation from the mean. The square root of about 481.1 is about 21.9 minutes -- roughly how far a typical delivery time sits from the 30.9-minute mean.

The standard deviation is expressed in the same units as the original data, while the variance is expressed in squared units; the range is based only on the two most extreme values and ignores how the rest of the data are spread. That's why "about 21.9 minutes" (the standard deviation) is easier to interpret directly than "about 481.1 minutes squared" (the variance) -- and why the range (62 minutes) says nothing about whether the other five delivery times are bunched tightly or scattered widely.

Range, variance, and standard deviation all quantify spread, but the range only looks at the two extremes, while variance and standard deviation take every observation's distance from the mean into account -- with standard deviation, unlike variance, expressed in the original units, and so usually the easiest to talk about in context.

coverage.learning_objective: Describe a distribution's shape as symmetric, right-skewed, or left-skewed, and explain what that shape implies about how the mean and median compare.

required_facts.statement: A distribution is right-skewed when it has a longer tail trailing off to the right, and left-skewed when it has a longer tail trailing off to the left.
A distribution is symmetric when it trails off by roughly equal amounts in both directions.
The mean is more affected by extreme observations, such as those in the long tail of a skewed distribution, than the median, which is more robust to them.

teaching_blocks.content: Look at a different batch of delivery times, this one trailing off gradually: 18, 20, 22, 22, 26, 28, 34, 41, 52 minutes. Most of the batch sits bunched between 18 and 28 minutes, and the remaining values increase step by step rather than jumping straight to one far-off value. That overall pattern -- where the bulk of the values sit and which direction, if any, the data trails off toward -- is what analysts call the shape of a distribution.

A distribution is right-skewed when it has a longer tail trailing off to the right, and left-skewed when it has a longer tail trailing off to the left. This delivery-time batch is right-skewed: the bulk of the values sit between 18 and 28 minutes, and 34, 41, and 52 form a gradually lengthening tail trailing off to the right.

A distribution is symmetric when it trails off by roughly equal amounts in both directions. If the batch instead had values spread evenly above and below its center -- say some deliveries a bit faster and some a bit slower than 24 minutes, with no single value trailing far off in either direction -- that would be a symmetric distribution instead.

The mean is more affected by extreme observations, such as those in the long tail of a skewed distribution, than the median, which is more robust to them. That's consistent with this batch: its mean (about 29.2 minutes) sits above its median (26 minutes), pulled upward by the gradual right-hand tail.

Describing a distribution's shape -- symmetric, right-skewed, or left-skewed -- is about how the bulk of the values are arranged around the center and which direction, if any, a long tail points; it's a separate description from picking out any one extreme value by itself.

context.concept_name: Reading a frequency distribution/histogram in statistical terms

coverage.learning_objective: Read a histogram or frequency table and describe what it shows about a dataset's distribution, including its modal range and any visible skew.

required_facts.statement: A histogram groups numerical values into bins and represents the count of observations in each bin as a bar; taller bars show where the data values are relatively more common.
A mode appears in a histogram as a prominent peak: a bin, or region of neighboring bins, where observations are noticeably more concentrated than elsewhere.
The table of counts of observations in each bin, which a histogram displays as bars, is called a frequency table.

teaching_blocks.content: Instead of listing every delivery time one by one, imagine grouping a full day's 21 deliveries into 10-minute ranges and counting how many orders fall into each range.

A histogram groups numerical values into bins and represents the count of observations in each bin as a bar; taller bars show where the data values are relatively more common. For the day's 21 deliveries, the tallest bar would sit over the 20-30 minute bin, and a much shorter bar would sit far out over the 80-90 minute bin.

The table of counts of observations in each bin, which a histogram displays as bars, is called a frequency table. For that same day, the frequency table might read: 10-20 minutes, 4 orders; 20-30 minutes, 9 orders; 30-40 minutes, 5 orders; 40-50 minutes, 2 orders; 50-80 minutes, 0 orders; 80-90 minutes, 1 order.

A mode appears in a histogram as a prominent peak: a bin, or region of neighboring bins, where observations are noticeably more concentrated than elsewhere. In the frequency table above, the 20-30 minute bin, with 9 of the 21 orders, is that peak.

Reading a histogram or frequency table means translating bar heights, or bin counts, back into statements about the data: where deliveries cluster most, and where the rare, far-out ones sit -- in this case, a strong cluster around 20-30 minutes with a single delivery trailing far out past 80 minutes.

coverage.learning_objective: Given a correlation coefficient value for two numeric variables, read its sign and magnitude to state the direction and relative strength of their linear relationship.

required_facts.statement: Correlation, which always takes values between -1 and 1, describes the strength of the linear relationship between two numeric variables.

In a positive association, higher values of one variable tend to go with higher values of the other; in a negative association, higher values of one variable tend to go with lower values of the other.

A correlation near +1 indicates a strong positive linear relationship, a correlation near -1 indicates a strong negative linear relationship, and a correlation near 0 indicates little or no linear relationship.

misconceptions.statement: Correlation quantifies the strength of a linear relationship only; a nonlinear relationship can be strong even when its correlation value looks weak.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose two numeric columns are recorded for many delivery orders: distance in kilometers, and delivery time in minutes. Do longer distances tend to go with longer delivery times?
Correlation, which always takes values between -1 and 1, describes the strength of the linear relationship between two numeric variables.

In a positive association, higher values of one variable tend to go with higher values of the other; in a negative association, higher values of one variable tend to go with lower values of the other. For distance and delivery time, a positive association would mean farther orders tend to take longer; a negative association would look different -- for example, if drivers-on-shift and delivery time have a correlation of about -0.65, that means more drivers on shift tends to go with shorter delivery times.

A correlation near +1 indicates a strong positive linear relationship, a correlation near -1 indicates a strong negative linear relationship, and a correlation near 0 indicates little or no linear relationship. Suppose the correlation between distance and delivery time in this dataset comes out to 0.82 -- close to +1, so distance and delivery time have a strong positive linear relationship: farther deliveries tend to take longer.

Correlation quantifies the strength of a linear relationship only; a nonlinear relationship can be strong even when its correlation value looks weak. So a correlation near 0 between two variables doesn't automatically mean they're unrelated -- it may mean their relationship isn't a straight-line one.
Reading a correlation value means reading its sign for direction and how close it sits to -1, 0, or +1 for strength -- without needing to recompute anything from the raw data yourself.

context.concept_name: Comparing correlation strength across multiple variable pairs

coverage.learning_objective: Compare several correlation coefficients to identify the strongest and weakest relationships, and explain why a strong pairwise correlation alone does not rule out a confounding variable.

required_facts.statement: The strength of a correlation is judged by its magnitude (absolute value): the closer the value is to 1, the stronger the linear relationship, regardless of whether the sign is positive or negative.

A confounding variable is a variable that is correlated with both of two other variables being studied, so it can produce an association between those two variables that is not a direct link between them.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose three numeric variables are recorded for the same delivery orders -- distance in kilometers, package weight in kilograms, and delivery time in minutes -- and their pairwise correlations come out to: distance and delivery time, 0.82; weight and delivery time, -0.41; distance and weight, -0.38.

The strength of a correlation is judged by its magnitude (absolute value): the closer the value is to 1, the stronger the linear relationship, regardless of whether the sign is positive or negative. Comparing the three values above by magnitude, 0.82 (distance and delivery time) is the strongest relationship and -0.38 (distance and weight) is the weakest -- even though -0.41 (weight and delivery time) is the lowest number of the three, its magnitude makes it slightly stronger than -0.38.

A confounding variable is a variable that is correlated with both of two other variables being studied, so it can produce an association between those two variables that is not a direct link between them. Here, distance is correlated with both weight and delivery time -- farther orders might tend to be lighter parcels, and also tend to take longer -- so the -0.41 correlation between weight and delivery time doesn't by itself mean weight and delivery time are directly linked; distance could be behind both.

Comparing magnitudes across a set of correlations tells you which relationships are relatively stronger or weaker, but a strong pairwise correlation on its own never rules out a third variable driving both sides of that pair.

coverage.learning_objective: Apply the correlation-vs-causation caveat when interpreting a business finding, flagging and rewriting claims that overstate what a correlational finding supports.

required_facts.statement: Association does not imply causation: a correlation between two variables does not by itself establish that one causes the other.
When only observational (correlational) data supports a finding, it should be restated as an association, or as a hypothesis to check later, rather than as a causal claim.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose an analysis finds that orders placed with the delivery app's "priority" toggle switched on correlate with faster delivery times.

Association does not imply causation: a correlation between two variables does not by itself establish that one causes the other. Finding that priority orders and fast deliveries move together in the data doesn't by itself prove that flipping the toggle is what speeds things up.

When only observational (correlational) data supports a finding, it should be restated as an association, or as a hypothesis to check later, rather than as a causal claim. So instead of writing "using priority delivery causes faster delivery," the honest version is closer to "priority orders and faster delivery times tend to occur together in this data; whether the toggle itself speeds things up is worth checking further" -- since, for example, priority orders might simply tend to come from closer neighborhoods.
Before writing up a correlational finding, check whether the wording claims a cause; if the data is only observational, restate it as an association instead of a causal claim.

coverage.learning_objective: Describe pandas' Series and DataFrame structures and how they relate, and construct a Series from a list and a DataFrame from a dict of lists.

required_facts.statement: A pandas Series is a one-dimensional labeled array that can hold data of any type; its axis labels are collectively called the index.
A pandas DataFrame is a two-dimensional labeled data structure whose columns can hold different types, and it can be thought of as a dict of Series objects that share an index.

A pandas Series can be constructed from data that is array-like, an Iterable (such as a Python list), a dict, or a scalar value. When built from a list (or other array-like data) with no index passed, the index defaults to 0, 1, ..., len(data) - 1; when built from a dict, the dict's keys become the index.
A DataFrame can be constructed from a dict of equal-length lists, where each key becomes a column name and each list becomes that column's values.
A DataFrame can be treated like a dict of like-indexed Series: df['col'] gets a column, and df['new'] = ... sets (or adds) a column, using the same syntax as the analogous dict operations.

teaching_blocks.content: Every pandas table starts from two building blocks. A pandas Series is a one-dimensional labeled array that can hold data of any type; its axis labels are collectively called the index.

A pandas Series can be constructed from data that is array-like, an Iterable (such as a Python list), a dict, or a scalar value. When built from a list (or other array-like data) with no index passed, the index defaults to 0, 1, ..., len(data) - 1; when built from a dict, the dict's keys become the index. `pd.Series([18, 20, 22, 22, 26, 28, 80])` -- built from a plain Python list of delivery times with no index passed -- defaults its labels to 0, 1, ..., 6. `pd.Series({"Lagos": 18, "Abuja": 20, "Kano": 26})`, built from a dict, instead uses "Lagos", "Abuja", and "Kano" as the index.
A pandas DataFrame is a two-dimensional labeled data structure whose columns can hold different types, and it can be thought of as a dict of Series objects that share an index.

A DataFrame can be constructed from a dict of equal-length lists, where each key becomes a column name and each list becomes that column's values: `orders = pd.DataFrame({"order_id": [1001, 1002, 1003], "city": ["Lagos", "Abuja", "Kano"], "delivery_time_minutes": [18, 20, 26]})` builds a three-column, three-row orders table this way.

A DataFrame can be treated like a dict of like-indexed Series: `df['col']` gets a column, and `df['new'] = ...` sets (or adds) a column, using the same syntax as the analogous dict operations. `orders['city']` gets the city column back as a Series, and `orders['courier'] = ['Ada', 'Bayo', 'Chidi']` adds a new column, using exactly the syntax you'd use to read or write a dict entry.

A DataFrame's column, once pulled out with `orders['delivery_time_minutes']`, is itself a Series -- the same one-dimensional, indexed structure this concept started with, now sharing the DataFrame's index.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose you want the city and delivery time for a particular order, or the first three rows regardless of their labels -- pandas gives two different accessors depending on how you want to address the data.
.loc selects data primarily by label (row or column names), while .iloc selects data primarily by integer position, from 0 to length-1 of the axis.

Both .loc and .iloc select using a row selector and a column selector separated by a comma (e.g. df.loc[rows, cols]); an axis left out of the selection, or given as a colon (:), means "all of that axis", so `orders.loc[3]` is equivalent to `orders.loc[3, :]` -- both return every column for the row labeled 3.
`orders.loc[2:4, "city"]` selects the city column for the rows labeled 2 through 4.

.loc slicing with labels (e.g. 'a':'f') includes both the start and the stop labels in the result, unlike ordinary Python slicing where the stop is excluded. So `orders.loc[2:4]` returns the rows labeled 2, 3, and 4 -- three rows, not two.
`orders.iloc[0:3, 0:2]` selects, by pure position, the first three rows and first two columns.

.iloc uses 0-based positional indexing where, when slicing, the start position is included and the stop position is excluded, following ordinary Python/NumPy slicing rules. So `orders.iloc[0:3]` returns positions 0, 1, and 2 -- three rows, matching normal Python slicing behavior.

The boundary rule flips between the two accessors -- .loc's label slices include the stop label, .iloc's position slices exclude the stop position -- which is worth double-checking any time a slice's row count looks off by one.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose you want the average delivery time per city, not for the whole batch of orders at once.

Group by refers to a process involving one or more of the following steps: splitting the data into groups based on some criteria, applying a function to each group independently, and combining the results into a data structure -- split every order into its city's group, apply "average" within each group, then combine the per-city averages into one result.
An aggregation is a groupby operation that reduces each group to a single summary value per column, such as computing the sum of a column within each group.

In practice, you call df.groupby(key) and then an aggregation method such as .sum() or .mean() on the DataFrame or a selected column, or .agg([...]) to compute several aggregations at once; by default the group keys become the index of the result: `orders.groupby("city")["delivery_time_minutes"].mean()` returns one average delivery time per city, with the city names as the index; `orders.groupby("city")["delivery_time_minutes"].agg(["mean", "sum"])` computes both the average and the total in one call.
Split, apply, combine is the whole idea -- groupby just gives you one call that does all three steps for whatever key and aggregation you choose.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose a wide summary table has one row per city and separate columns "jan_deliveries", "feb_deliveries", "mar_deliveries" -- and you need one row per city-month combination instead.

melt() reshapes a DataFrame from wide to long format: the columns listed as id_vars stay as identifier columns, while all other columns are unpivoted into two columns, one holding the original column names and one holding their values: `city_deliveries.melt(id_vars=["city"])` keeps "city" as an identifier and turns "jan_deliveries", "feb_deliveries", and "mar_deliveries" into two new columns -- one holding those original column names, the other holding each of their counts.

The default 'variable' and 'value' column names produced by melt() can be renamed using its var_name and value_name parameters: `city_deliveries.melt(id_vars=["city"], var_name="month", value_name="deliveries")` gives those two new columns clearer names.

required_facts.statement: pivot_table() reshapes data by turning the distinct values of one column into new columns, and unlike plain pivot(), it can handle duplicate index/column combinations by aggregating the numeric values.
pivot_table() takes index, columns, and values arguments: index sets the rows of the output table, columns sets the new columns, and values selects which column(s) to aggregate into the table.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the long table that melt produced earlier is saved as long_deliveries, with one row per city-month and the columns city, month, and deliveries -- and it needs to go back to a wide table: cities as rows, months as columns.

pivot_table() reshapes data by turning the distinct values of one column into new columns, and unlike plain pivot(), it can handle duplicate index/column combinations by aggregating the numeric values.

pivot_table() takes index, columns, and values arguments: index sets the rows of the output table, columns sets the new columns, and values selects which column(s) to aggregate into the table: `long_deliveries.pivot_table(index="city", columns="month", values="deliveries")` puts each city on its own row, each month as its own column, and the delivery counts as the values filling the grid.

pivot_table() combines rows that share the same index/column values using aggfunc, which defaults to 'mean'; passing aggfunc='sum' (or another function) changes how those values are combined -- so if a city had two rows for the same month, the default call above would average them instead of erroring, and adding aggfunc="sum" would total them instead.
pivot_table spreads long data wider by turning one column's values into new column headers, aggregating whenever more than one row lands in the same cell.
